title: Full-root and normalizer data extend to a reductive group homomorphism
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P=(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Use the root subgroups $U_\gamma$, exponentials $\exp_\gamma$, Weyl representatives $n_\alpha$, reflections $s_\alpha$, orders $m_{\alpha\beta}$, torus elements $t_{\alpha\beta}$ and positive two-root subgroups $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$ of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. An affine $A$-group scheme is an affine scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams; all homomorphisms below preserve those operations. Let $H$ be such a group. Let $N=N_G(T)$ denote the normalizer subgroup scheme: its points normalize $T$ after every further algebra extension. For $\alpha\in\Delta$, put $L_\alpha=M\cap\mathbf Q\alpha$ and $S_\alpha=D_A(M/L_\alpha)\subseteq T$, and let $K_\alpha=Z_G(S_\alpha)$ denote the rank-one centralizer subgroup scheme; its points commute with $S_\alpha$ after every further algebra extension. Give homomorphisms $f_N:N\to H$ and $g_\gamma:U_\gamma\to H$ for every root, satisfying $$f_N(n)g_\gamma(u)f_N(n)^{-1}=g_{w\gamma}(nun^{-1})$$ after every commutative $A$-algebra extension, for every normalizer point $n$ with Weyl image $w$ and $u\in U_\gamma$, interpreted componentwise when $w$ is locally constant. Suppose for each simple $\alpha$ there is a homomorphism $F_\alpha:K_\alpha\to H$ restricting to $g_\alpha,g_{-\alpha}$ on $U_\alpha,U_{-\alpha}$ and to $f_N$ on $N\cap K_\alpha$. Suppose also that for every distinct simple pair $\alpha,\beta$ there is a homomorphism $q_{\alpha\beta}:U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}\to H$ restricting to $g_c$ on every $U_c$ for $c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$. Then there is a unique homomorphism $f:G\to H$ extending $f_N$ and all the $g_\gamma$. Empty roots, arbitrary nonzero commutative $A$, and disconnected and nonreduced bases are permitted.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 and its proof, printed pp.198–200, full-root/normalizer criterion; strengthened by requiring normalizer equivariance for every normalizer point rather than just simple representatives. proof.text: If $\Phi$ is empty, the root-calculus statement gives $G=T$ and $N=G$, so take $f=f_N$; uniqueness follows from the required restriction. Henceforth allow any nonempty $\Phi$. We will construct homomorphisms on both $U_{\Phi^+}$ and $U_{-\Phi^+}$. Fix either sign and write $\Sigma$ for that positive system. Choose a rational linear functional $\ell$ positive on $\Sigma$ with distinct values on its roots: start with signed height in the simple-root basis and perturb by a sufficiently small rational functional avoiding the finitely many hyperplanes $\ell(a-b)=0$. Extend it across the central complement in $M_{\mathbf Q}$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 opening uniqueness argument, p.198; Lemma 6.2.3 ordering, p.199; explicit choice of order and empty-root check by Q104.

proof.text:
For distinct $a,b\in\Sigma$, reducedness makes $a,b$ linearly independent. Put $\Xi=\Phi\cap(\mathbf Qa+\mathbf Qb)\cap\Sigma$. The root-plane lemma gives $w$ carrying $\Xi$ onto $\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$ for two distinct simple roots. Since that lemma gives $w$ as a product of simple reflections $s_{d_1}\cdots s_{d_k}$, put $n=n_{d_1}\cdots n_{d_k}$; by root calculus each $n_d$ has Weyl image $s_d$ and conjugates $U_c$ onto $U_{s_dc}$, so $n$ has Weyl image $w$. Conjugation by $n$ identifies $U_\Xi$ with $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$: on every root factor it carries $U_c$ to $U_{wc}$, and the ordered-product isomorphisms identify the whole subgroup. Therefore
$$Q_{a,b}(z)=f_N(n)^{-1}q_{\alpha\beta}(nzn^{-1})f_N(n)$$
is a homomorphism $U_\Xi\to H$. Normalizer equivariance in the hypothesis gives $Q_{a,b}|_{U_c}=g_c$ for every $c\in\Xi$. Consequently its value on every ordered root-factor decomposition in $U_\Xi$ is the product of the corresponding $g_c$ values. This construction works for the negative system too, since the root-plane lemma permits any $\ell$.

source.place: Lemma 6.2.3 proof, p.200: rank-two reduction and conjugation; Q104 uses the full positive root-plane subgroup supplied by the stronger hypotheses.

proof.text:
Enumerate $\Sigma=\{c_1,\ldots,c_m\}$ by strictly increasing $\ell$. Set $V_i=U_{\{c_i,\ldots,c_m\}}$, $V_{m+1}=1$, and let $P_i:V_i\to H$ be the morphism defined by the increasing ordered product of the $g_c$. These tail root sets are closed: the $\ell$-value of a sum of at least two roots in a tail is larger than either summand. Root calculus gives their subgroup structures and product coordinates. Multiplying $\ell$ by a positive common denominator of its values on a basis of $M$ gives a homomorphism $\lambda:M\to\mathbf Z$ with $\Sigma=\{c\in\Phi:\lambda(c)>0\}$. The commutator-support theorem applies to this $\lambda$ after choosing generators of the free root lines and the resulting exponential parametrizations; root calculus supplies their closed immersions and $T$-equivariance. For $a=c_j>b=c_i$ and root points $x\in U_a$, $y\in U_b$, it gives
$$y^{-1}xy\in U_a\,U_{\{ka+lb\in\Phi:k,l>0\}}\subset V_{i+1}.$$
Indeed $[y^{-1},x]$ has precisely the stated mixed-root support, and each mixed root has $\ell$-value greater than $\ell(a)$. This also proves that $U_{c_i}$ normalizes $V_{i+1}$. All factors in the displayed element lie in $\Xi$ of step 2. Thus, by evaluating its ordered coordinates using $Q_{a,b}$,
$$P_{i+1}(y^{-1}xy)=g_b(y)^{-1}g_a(x)g_b(y).$$

source.place: Lemma 6.2.3 proof, pp.199--200, equation (6.2.1); commutator support as in Conrad Proposition 5.1.14. Mixed-root support and tail bounds written out by Q104.

proof.text:
We prove $P_i$ is a homomorphism by descending induction. The base $P_{m+1}:1\to H$ is the identity-valued map. Assume $P_{i+1}$ is a homomorphism. Every point $v\in V_{i+1}$ is an ordered product of root points. Apply step 3 to these factors and use the homomorphism property on $V_{i+1}$ to obtain
$$P_{i+1}(y^{-1}vy)=g_{c_i}(y)^{-1}P_{i+1}(v)g_{c_i}(y)$$
for $y\in U_{c_i}$. Unique product coordinates give $V_i=U_{c_i}V_{i+1}$ and $P_i(xv)=g_{c_i}(x)P_{i+1}(v)$. Since
$$(xv)(yw)=(xy)(y^{-1}vy)w,$$
the last conjugation formula and the two homomorphism properties give
$$P_i((xv)(yw))=g_{c_i}(x)P_{i+1}(v)g_{c_i}(y)P_{i+1}(w)=P_i(xv)P_i(yw).$$
The identity is sent to the identity; inverses are then preserved as well. All equalities hold naturally on every algebra, hence are scheme-morphism identities. This completes the induction for each sign and constructs $F_\pm:U_{\pm\Phi^+}\to H$ restricting to every prescribed $g_c$. Since these are homomorphisms, their formulas are products of $g_c$ in any root enumeration, by root calculus.

source.place: Lemma 6.2.3 descending induction, pp.199--200; explicit semidirect-product computation, for each sign, by Q104.

proof.text: Apply the Weyl-cell compatibility lemma to $f_N$ and the homomorphisms $F_\pm$ just constructed. Its root restrictions are exactly $g_c$, so its normalizer-equivariance hypothesis is the given one, including locally constant Weyl images over disconnected test rings. Take its $E_\alpha$ to be the supplied $F_\alpha$; the restrictions on opposite roots and $N\cap K_\alpha$ are precisely the hypotheses of this item. We obtain an open cover $G=\bigcup_w C_w$, maps $a_w:C_w\to H$ agreeing on every intersection, and the multiplication identity on each $(C_w\times C_z)\cap\mu^{-1}(C_r)$. The substantive word-length/gluing calculation is this separate cited input; no Bruhat stratification of algebra-valued points is used.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 proof, p.199: the Weyl-word induction following construction of the unipotent homomorphisms.

proof.text: Scheme-morphism gluing gives a unique morphism $f:G\to H$ restricting to the $a_w$. The opens $(C_w\times C_z)\cap\mu^{-1}(C_r)$ cover $G\times_A G$, so their multiplication identities give $f\circ\mu=\mu_H\circ(f\times f)$ by the equality clause of the gluing theorem. In $C_1=\Omega$ the formula gives $f(1)=1$; multiplication and identity imply preservation of inverse. On the root groups and on $T$ the formula for $a_1$ gives $g_c$ and $f_T$. On $Tn_w\subset C_w$, write $tn_w=n_w(n_w^{-1}tn_w)$ to get $a_w(tn_w)=f_N(tn_w)$. The quotient $N/T$ and the representatives identify $N$ with the disjoint union of these cosets (locally on open-and-closed parts over test rings), so $f|_N=f_N$. Finally any homomorphism with the prescribed restrictions must satisfy the displayed formula for $a_w$ on $C_w$, by its homomorphism property and the open-cell product coordinates. The equality clause of gluing therefore proves uniqueness. Every argument was over arbitrary $A$-algebras and required no reduction or connectedness assumption.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.1 uniqueness and open-cell argument, pp.198--199; final gluing and group-diagram verification by Q104.

Glued their cell maps and checked all group diagrams, full normalizer restrictions, uniqueness and empty roots.
